newsitem.title: ROMANIA: LEADING PARTIES IN ROMANIA'S PARLIAMENTARY POLL.
newsitem.headline: LEADING PARTIES IN ROMANIA'S PARLIAMENTARY POLL.

text.p: Romania's parliamentary election on Sunday, which takes place alongside voting for a new president, will settle who sits in the 341 seats in the lower Chamber of Deputies and 143 seats in the Senate.
Opinion polls suggest there will be no clear winner in the race for the presidency, forcing a run-off vote on November 17.
But the parliamentary vote may give Romania's opposition parties their first chance to form a government since communism fell in 1989.

Opinion polls put the Democratic Convention bloc of Emil Constantinescu ahead of President Ion Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy, with ex-premier Petre Roman's Social Democratic Union likely to hold the balance of power.
Thousands of candidates from 27 parties, five alliances and 34 ethnic associations representing 18 ethnic minorities, are fighting for seats in the country's legislative assemblies.
Here are profiles of the top parties.

PARTY OF SOCIAL DEMOCRACY (PDSR) - Born out of the remnants of the National Salvation Front, which was formed after the 1989 anti-communist revolution and fell apart in 1992, the PDSR is the party of Romania's leftist ruling elite.
Under Iliescu the NSF/PDSR has been at the heart of all governing coalitions since Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was ousted.

But voter disgust at corruption, abuse of privilege and economic mismanagement could end its period at the helm. It is running second in the opinion polls with around 28 percent and main opposition parties may combine in coalition against it.
The PDSR promises gradual economic reform that will protect workers from the pain of modernising Romania's antiquated industry and agriculture. Its support is strongest in rural areas.
DEMOCRATIC CONVENTION (CDR) - The CDR, an alliance of 15 centrist opposition parties whose presidential candidate is Emil Constantinescu, has its best chance yet of winning power.
The CDR, formed in 1991, has run a solid campaign after making inroads into PDSR heartlands in spring municipal elections. It averages around 32 percent in opinion polls.
The CDR has campaigned on an anti-corruption platform, pledged to hasten economic reform and respect the rule of law.
It says that Romania has fallen behind its neighbours under Iliescu and will be kept out of NATO and the European Union for years unless it tackles stagnation and decay with more vigour.
The PDSR has tagged the CDR as closet monarchists, a charge with weight in republican Romania, but one that appears not to have stuck.

SOCIAL DEMOCRATIC UNION (USD) - With pollsters giving ex-premier and presidential candidate Petre Roman's USD around 18 percent the reformist free-marketeers could play a key role in deciding the shape of Romania's next government.
The CDR are the USD's natural allies but there appears to be little love between the two groups.

The USD's pro-European, modernising programme, which appeals to the urban young, is close to the CDR's promise of a fresh start for Romania and what keeps the two apart are the personalities of their leaders, analysts say. REUTER
